name: Cold compress / chilled washcloth

angle.text: Users hold a chilled cloth or gel pack on closed eyes after waking to bring down morning puffiness and look more rested. Cold therapy is studied for other uses, while its effect on eye bags specifically is based on anecdote.

summary: A chilled cloth or pack held on the eyes to reduce morning puffiness; cold therapy has broader evidence, but not for eyes specifically.
note: Avoid direct ice on skin; cold injury is documented in cold therapy devices.
currentQuick:
A cold compress or chilled washcloth is a simple way people try to reduce puffiness around the eyes. The cold is said to narrow vessels and limit fluid.
Cold therapy has been studied for injury and post-surgical swelling, with mixed results, but no trial was found on cosmetic under-eye puffiness.
How it works: Cold lowers tissue temperature and causes vasoconstriction; compression limits fluid leaking from vessels. In sustained cold, a cycle of vasoconstriction followed by vasodilation can occur.
Risks and caveats: Ice applied directly to skin can cause a cold burn, and uncontrolled cooling devices have been linked to frostbite and severe tissue damage. A cloth barrier is described as safer.
deepLead:
A cold compress or chilled washcloth is a home practice of holding a cold, damp cloth, gel pack or similar item against the closed eyes to reduce puffiness, often after waking.
Cold therapy generally is used for pain and swelling after soft-tissue injury and some surgeries, including facial surgery. Cold lowers tissue temperature and constricts vessels, while compression limits fluid leakage. Evidence for cryotherapy is mixed, and one systematic review found insufficient evidence in ankle sprains.
No clinical study of cold compresses for cosmetic periorbital puffiness was found; the evidence above concerns injuries and surgery.

name: Lymphatic drainage eye massage

angle.text: Users stroke lightly around the eyes to move fluid and reduce under-eye puffiness. The technique is adapted from manual lymphatic drainage, which has mixed evidence in lymphedema, and its use for eye bags is untested.

summary: Light fingertip strokes around the eyes meant to move fluid and reduce puffiness; adapted from manual lymphatic drainage, which has mixed evidence even in lymphedema.
note: Evidence is for lymphedema, not cosmetic eye puffiness.
currentQuick:
Lymphatic drainage eye massage uses very light, rhythmic strokes around the eye area to encourage fluid to drain. It is borrowed from manual lymphatic drainage, a therapy developed in the 1930s.
Research on the technique centers on lymphedema and is mixed; none was found on cosmetic eye puffiness.
How it works: The premise is that gentle skin stretching moves lymph toward lymph nodes. Pressure is light, under about 4 kPa, and applied with rhythmic circular movements.
Risks and caveats: No specific risk data for the eye-area version were found. As with any massage near the eyes, vigorous rubbing is a concern in dark-circle literature, where eye rubbing is linked to inflammation and pigmentation.
deepLead:
Lymphatic drainage eye massage is a practice of gentle, light-pressure strokes around the eyes and face intended to move fluid and reduce puffiness. It is adapted from manual lymphatic drainage (MLD).
MLD was developed by Danish practitioners Emil and Estrid Vodder in the 1930s, initially for chronic sinusitis, and was introduced in Paris in 1936. It is described as light rhythmic skin manipulation rather than conventional massage.
Research on MLD concerns lymphedema, with mixed results; a 2013 systematic review on breast cancer-related lymphedema found no clear support for preventing or treating swelling, while a 2022 study reported improved lymphedema with new collateral pathways. No study of eye-area drainage massage for cosmetic puffiness was found.

name: Eye yoga / eye exercises

angle.text: Practitioners say routines of eye movements, palming and focus shifting relieve strain and firm or brighten the skin around the eyes. The practice descends from the Bates method, and no studies have tested an appearance effect.

summary: Eye movement and relaxation routines claimed to firm the eye area; no studies support an appearance effect.
note: Related Bates-method practices such as sungazing carry documented risks.
currentQuick:
Eye yoga is a set of eye-movement and relaxation routines. Some in looksmaxxing circles say it firms or brightens the eye area.
No studies were found testing this. Reviews of eye exercises for vision itself found no clear benefit.
How it works: Practitioners move or rest the eyes through set routines, on the theory that this relieves strain or tone in the surrounding muscles.
Risks and caveats: Plain eye movements are low-risk, but related Bates-method practices like sungazing or pressing on the eyes have documented risks, and abandoning glasses can be unsafe.
deepLead:
Eye yoga, or eye exercises, refers to routines of deliberate eye movements, palming, focus shifting and relaxation that practitioners say can relieve strain, improve vision and, in looksmaxxing circles, firm or brighten the skin around the eyes. The practice draws on a lineage that includes the Bates method, an alternative therapy developed by the American eye doctor William Horatio Bates (1860-1931).
Reviews of the vision-training literature have not found objective evidence that eye exercises improve eyesight; an American Academy of Ophthalmology review and a 2005 review of 43 studies reported no clear benefit for visual acuity. No published study found in the sources reviewed has tested eye exercises for the appearance of the skin or tissues around the eyes.

name: Lemon / tomato juice for dark circles

angle.text: Online communities apply lemon or tomato juice under the eyes as a home lightener for dark circles, crediting vitamin C and lycopene. The lightening effect on periorbital circles is untested.

summary: A DIY acid lightener for under-eye circles; untested, and citrus plus sun can cause lasting dark marks.
note: Citrus juice on skin in sunlight is linked to phytophotodermatitis.
currentQuick:
People apply lemon or tomato juice under the eyes hoping to lighten dark circles, citing vitamin C and acidity.
No studies were found testing this use.
How it works: Proponents say the acids and vitamin C lighten pigment. No research has examined this on under-eye skin.
Risks and caveats: Citrus on skin followed by sun exposure can cause phytophotodermatitis, which may leave brown marks lasting years. Skin near the eye is thin and sensitive.
deepLead:
Applying lemon juice or tomato juice under the eyes is a do-it-yourself remedy that online communities say lightens periorbital dark circles. Lemon is acidic and rich in vitamin C, while tomato juice contains lycopene and vitamin C, and proponents credit these for a "lightening" effect.
No published trials were found testing lemon or tomato juice on dark circles. Dermatology sources list thin skin, pigment, vessels, allergies and sleep loss as causes, and report that citrus juice on skin exposed to sunlight can cause phytophotodermatitis, a reaction that may leave lasting dark marks.

name: Screen time / blue light reduction

chain: Less screen strain and late light
angle.text: Users cut screen time or use blue-light filters to ease eye strain and the tired look around the eyes. Trials of blue-blocking glasses are mostly negative for eye strain, and the appearance effect is untested.

summary: Cutting screen time or blue light to ease eye strain; trials of blue-blockers are mostly negative and appearance effects are untested.
currentQuick:
Reducing screens or blue light is said to ease eye strain and tired-looking eyes.
Trials of blue-blocking lenses mostly found no help for eye strain, and no study links this to appearance.
How it works: Breaks reduce sustained near focus; filters aim to cut blue wavelengths from screens.
Risks and caveats: Low risk. The main cost is time or the price of filter lenses.
deepLead:
Reducing screen time or blue light exposure, through breaks, filter glasses or night modes, is discussed in looksmaxxing circles as a way to ease eye strain and the tired look around the eyes. Computer vision syndrome describes eye strain, dryness, headache and blurred vision after prolonged screen use.
Randomised trials of blue-blocking lenses have mostly not found benefit for digital eye strain, and no studies were found linking screen time or blue light reduction to dark circles or other facial appearance.

name: Hypoallergenic bedding / dust mite control

angle.text: Looksmaxxing communities link dust mite allergens to morning facial puffiness and allergic-looking eyes, and use allergen-proof covers and hot washing to reduce them. The approach is established for dust allergy and untested for facial puffiness.

summary: Allergen-proof bedding to limit mites; useful for dust allergy, untested for facial puffiness.
currentQuick:
Mite-proof covers and hot washing reduce dust mite allergens.
Some link allergies to a puffy morning face, but no study tests bedding for appearance.
How it works: Covers and washing limit contact with mite allergens that trigger rhinitis and eye symptoms.
Risks and caveats: Low risk. Sources note partial covers need regular cleaning.
deepLead:
Hypoallergenic bedding and dust mite control means using allergen-proof covers, hot washing and humidity reduction to limit mite allergens, which looksmaxxing communities sometimes link to morning facial puffiness or allergic-looking eyes. House dust mites live in bedding and feed on shed skin, and are a common cause of allergic rhinitis and asthma.
Dust mite allergy itself is documented, and avoidance measures are described as reducing exposure; no studies were found testing bedding changes for facial appearance.

name: Creatine water retention concerns

chain: Worry about extra water in face
angle.text: Users who take creatine for muscle gain worry that it bloats the face. Reviews describe the early weight gain as water moving into muscle, mainly during loading, and facial effects have not been studied.

summary: Whether creatine puffs the face; water goes into muscle per reviews, facial effects untested.
currentQuick:
Some users worry creatine bloats the face.
References describe water entering muscle; no studies address the face.
How it works: Creatine raises muscle creatine and draws water in by osmosis.
Risks and caveats: Reviews report no kidney harm in studied groups; safety data are lacking for children and pregnancy.
deepLead:
Creatine water retention concerns refers to worries in looksmaxxing communities that creatine supplements cause facial bloating or puffiness. Reference sources describe early weight gain from creatine as water moving into muscle, mainly during loading.
Long-term studies are described as suggesting creatine does not necessarily change total body water relative to muscle mass. No studies were found specifically on creatine and facial appearance.

name: Elevated head sleeping / wedge pillow

angle.text: Users sleep with the head raised on a wedge pillow or bed risers to wake with a less puffy face. Head-of-bed elevation is an established measure for reflux, while its effect on facial puffiness is untested.

summary: Raising the head while asleep to cut morning puffiness; proven for reflux, untested for looks.
currentQuick:
Wedge pillows raise the head during sleep. They are used for reflux.
Some say they reduce morning facial puffiness; no trial tests this.
How it works: Elevation is thought to limit fluid shifting toward the face while lying flat.
Risks and caveats: Low risk; one reflux trial and a review exist, none on appearance.
deepLead:
Sleeping with the head raised, using a wedge pillow or bed risers, is said by looksmaxxing communities to reduce morning facial puffiness from fluid pooling. Head-of-bed elevation is an established lifestyle measure for reflux.
Reference sources suggest elevation may limit fluid shifting around the eyes, but no trials were found testing wedge pillows for facial appearance.

name: Lymphatic drainage massage

angle.text: Users massage the face lightly to move lymph fluid and debloat it for more definition, and some do it several times a day. Clinical research on manual lymphatic drainage centers on lymphedema, and the facial use rests on anecdote.

summary: Light-pressure facial and body massage meant to move fluid along lymph pathways; popular for 'debloating' the face, with clinical research limited to lymphedema.
note: Published clinical research concerns lymphedema; no controlled studies of facial 'definition' effects were found.
currentQuick:
Lymphatic drainage massage uses very light, rhythmic strokes intended to encourage lymph, the fluid that collects between tissues, to move toward lymph nodes. In looksmaxxing communities it is mostly discussed as a way to reduce facial puffiness, and is often combined with gua sha, jump rope or other 'debloating' habits.
The technique was developed in the 1930s by Emil and Estrid Vodder for sinus and immune complaints. Its established clinical use today is in lymphedema, where studies have returned mixed results. Posts on looksmax.org describe the face as changing through 'fluid redistribution' rather than fat loss.
How it works: Practitioners apply light pressure (under roughly 4 kPa) in circular, rhythmic movements directed toward lymph node regions. The underlying hypothesis is that this stimulates lymph flow and drains excess interstitial fluid. Forum guides adapt it into self-massage routines, sometimes with a gua sha tool.
Risks and caveats: Light massage is generally described as low-risk, though clinical sources define contraindications (for example certain infections or heart conditions) that apply to professional treatment. Forum users with acne or other skin problems are told by some posters to avoid icing or tools afterward. No published study has measured facial appearance outcomes.
deepLead:
Lymphatic drainage massage, usually called manual lymphatic drainage (MLD), is a form of gentle skin manipulation based on the hypothesis that it encourages lymph to move away from tissues toward the heart. Practitioners use light pressure and slow, rhythmic circular movements rather than the deeper pressure of conventional massage.
The method was developed by the Danish practitioners Emil and Estrid Vodder, who began working out the hand movements in 1932 after noticing swollen lymph nodes in patients with chronic colds. They presented it in Paris in 1936 and taught it in Copenhagen after the Second World War. The specific clinical application most often named for MLD is lymphedema, where research results have been mixed.
In looksmaxxing communities, lymphatic drainage is discussed mainly as a free or low-cost way to reduce facial puffiness and sharpen jawline and cheek definition, often alongside gua sha, cardio and cutting salt. Proponents describe the effect as fluid redistribution rather than fat loss. No published controlled study has examined MLD for cosmetic facial changes.

name: Face yoga / face exercises

angle.text: Users repeat facial muscle movements and massage to tone the face, look younger and reduce puffiness. Small studies exist on appearance changes, though good evidence is limited.

summary: Repeated facial-muscle movements promoted for toning and de-puffing the face; small studies exist but good evidence for appearance changes is limited.
note: Available trials are small, and studies on puffiness are mostly in surgical or TMD patients rather than healthy people.
currentQuick:
Face yoga refers to routines of facial muscle contractions, stretches and massage-like movements. It is marketed for anti-aging and, in looksmaxxing circles, for reducing puffiness and improving facial tone.
Published research is sparse. There is a 2014 systematic review of facial exercises for rejuvenation, a small 2025 pre-experimental study in 12 middle-aged women, and trials in other settings such as temporomandibular dysfunction and swelling after nose surgery.
How it works: Proponents propose that exercising facial muscles increases their tone and bulk and may help move fluid. Researchers have measured outcomes such as muscle tonus, stiffness and elasticity, but the proposed mechanisms for cosmetic changes remain under study.
Risks and caveats: Gentle facial exercise is not associated with major documented harms in the studies listed. Some people discussing the practice raise concern that repeated muscle contraction might deepen expression lines; no study cited here tested that.
deepLead:
Face yoga, also called face exercises, is a set of routines involving repeated contraction, stretching or massage of facial muscles. It is promoted as a non-surgical way to look younger, tone the face and reduce puffiness.
Published research is limited and small. A 2014 systematic review in Aesthetic Surgery Journal evaluated the literature on facial exercises for rejuvenation, framing the effectiveness of such approaches as still debated. A 2025 pre-experimental trial in Medicina studied 12 women with a mean age near 50 over eight weeks of intensive face yoga, measuring facial muscle tonus, stiffness and elasticity.
In looksmaxxing communities the practice is mentioned alongside lymphatic massage and gua sha as a way to reduce facial puffiness.

name: Low-sodium diet

angle.text: Users cut sodium to reduce water retention and facial puffiness. The diet is established medically for blood pressure, and its effect on facial appearance specifically is largely untested.

summary: Restricting dietary sodium, a medical strategy for blood pressure, also used in looksmaxxing circles to reduce water retention and facial puffiness.
note: Evidence is strongest for blood pressure; effects on facial appearance have not been directly studied in the sources reviewed.
currentQuick:
A low-sodium diet limits total sodium intake, commonly to 1,500 to 2,300 mg per day, mainly by cutting processed and packaged foods. It is a standard approach for managing hypertension and heart disease.
In looksmaxxing communities it is cited as a way to cut fluid retention that makes the face look puffy. Medical sources describe sodium's role in fluid balance and report short-term water-weight changes, but studies of facial appearance specifically were not found.
How it works: Sodium is the main positive ion in extracellular fluid and helps regulate blood volume and osmotic balance. Higher intake is associated with greater fluid retention and blood pressure, and reducing it lets the kidneys excrete more fluid.
Risks and caveats: Very low blood sodium (hyponatremia) can occur with excess body water; the physiological minimum is estimated at roughly 115 to 500 mg a day depending on sweating and activity. Clinicians advise individuals with heart or kidney conditions to follow medical guidance on sodium.
deepLead:
A low-sodium diet is an eating pattern that limits sodium intake, typically to between 1,500 and 2,300 mg per day. It is used in managing hypertension, heart failure and kidney disease, and it emphasizes fresh, unprocessed foods over packaged ones.
Sodium is the main positive ion in extracellular fluid and helps regulate blood volume, blood pressure and osmotic balance. Health organizations such as the American Heart Association recommend no more than 1,500 mg daily as an ideal limit for most adults, and the World Health Organization recommends under 2,000 mg, according to one reference source.
In looksmaxxing discussions, reducing salt is used as a way to reduce water retention and facial puffiness. No studies specifically tested this appearance outcome in the sources reviewed.

name: Gluten-free diet for bloat

angle.text: Users drop gluten hoping to cut bloating and facial puffiness. The diet is the accepted treatment for celiac disease, and no evidence was found for face-puff use in people without gluten-related conditions.

summary: Dropping gluten to cut bloating and facial puffiness; medically indicated for celiac disease, with no evidence found for face-puff use in people without gluten-related conditions.
note: Medical consensus advises testing for celiac disease before going gluten-free; no studies on facial puffiness were found.
currentQuick:
A gluten-free diet excludes the proteins found in wheat, barley and rye. It is the accepted treatment for celiac disease, and is used by some people with non-celiac gluten sensitivity. Among looksmaxxers, gluten elimination is proposed as a way to reduce bloating and facial puffiness.
In the sources reviewed, bloating appears as a symptom in non-celiac gluten sensitivity, and a 2018 crossover study suggested fructans may contribute more than gluten. No study of facial appearance was found.
How it works: For people with celiac disease, gluten triggers an immune reaction in the small intestine. In non-celiac gluten sensitivity, causes are unclear, with fructans and wheat proteins called ATIs proposed. Whether gluten affects the face in people without these conditions has not been studied.
Risks and caveats: Possible nutritional gaps (iron, B vitamins, folate, calcium, fiber), especially when processed gluten-free substitutes replace whole foods. Physicians generally advise testing for celiac disease before starting, since the diet can affect test accuracy.
deepLead:
A gluten-free diet excludes gluten, the group of proteins in wheat, barley, rye and related grains. Lifelong adherence is the only medically accepted treatment for celiac disease.
Beyond celiac disease, some people follow it for non-celiac gluten sensitivity, a condition described as controversial with unclear causes and an estimated prevalence of 0.5 to 13 percent. Since the early 21st century, the diet has also become popular as a lifestyle choice, including among athletes.
In appearance-focused communities, gluten elimination is proposed to reduce bloating and facial puffiness. No published studies on facial puffiness were found in the sources reviewed.

name: Water cutting / dehydration

angle.text: Users deliberately shed body water through fluid restriction, sweating and saunas to look leaner and more defined, a method borrowed from combat sports weight cuts. The short-term leaner look is visible, and the method is well documented in weigh-in sports.

summary: Deliberate fluid loss to look leaner or make weight; documented in combat sports, with dehydration-related deaths and regulator responses.
note: Associated with documented deaths in combat sports; dehydration can cause serious complications.
currentQuick:
Water cutting is the deliberate reduction of body water, often through sweating, saunas, sweatsuits or fluid manipulation, to lose weight quickly or look drier and leaner. It is best documented in combat sports, where athletes cut to a lower weight class before weigh-ins, and it is also referred to in bodybuilding contexts for a 'dry' look.
Sports medicine commentary cited here describes it as dangerous, and several athletes have died while cutting weight. Some organizations have changed their rules in response.
How it works: Methods described include restricting food and fluids, water-loading, exercise-induced sweating, sweatsuits and saunas. Because sweat is mostly water, weight lost this way is largely fluid, which returns with rehydration.
Risks and caveats: Dehydration can cause headache, fatigue, confusion, seizures, heatstroke, hypernatremia and kidney problems. Losses of 15 to 25 percent of body water are described as fatal. Deaths in weight-cutting athletes in 2015, 2016 and 2017 have been reported.
deepLead:
Water cutting is the practice of rapidly reducing body water, usually to make a lower weight class in combat sports or rowing, and in some communities to appear leaner. Methods include restricting food and fluids, water-loading, sweating through exercise, sweatsuits and saunas.
Dehydration is a deficit of total body water, with effects ranging from thirst and impaired cognition at 1 to 2 percent loss to deterioration at over 10 percent, and death at 15 to 25 percent. Weight-cutting writing in the sources described acute water loss as very dangerous and generally advised against by nutrition experts.
Documentation of the practice in bodybuilding and looksmaxxing circles is not covered in the sources reviewed here.

name: Cardio / sweating

angle.text: Users exercise to sweat out fluid for a leaner, less puffy look. Sweat is mostly water, so the physiology is known, while the effect on facial appearance has not been tested.

summary: Exercising to sweat out fluid for a leaner, less puffy look; sweat is mostly water, so the physiology is known but appearance effects are untested here.
note: Fluid lost through sweat is replaced by rehydration; heavy sweating in heat carries dehydration risk.
currentQuick:
The idea is to use cardio or heat to sweat out fluid and look leaner or less puffy. Sweat is a watery fluid released by eccrine glands to cool the body, and heavy exercise can produce large water losses.
The sources reviewed describe how sweat works but say nothing about facial appearance, and no studies on that outcome were found.
How it works: Exercise heats the muscles and increases sweating, which cools the skin as it evaporates. Sweat contains roughly 0.2 to 1 percent dissolved solutes including sodium, so sweating removes water and some electrolytes.
Risks and caveats: Heavy sweating can cause dehydration and electrolyte loss, with sodium depletion associated with cramps. Water-weight lost by sweating is typically temporary.
deepLead:
Sweating is the release of fluid by sweat glands, which in humans mainly regulates temperature. Heat and muscle exertion increase output, and sweat is mostly water with small amounts of sodium, potassium and other solutes.
During average-intensity exercise water losses can reach about 2 litres per hour, and adults can sweat 2 to 4 litres per hour at peak. In looksmaxxing contexts, cardio and sweating are described as a way to shed fluid for a leaner look. No studies on facial appearance were found in the sources reviewed.

name: Sauna / steam

angle.text: Users fold sauna and steam sessions into skincare and wellness routines for sweating, skin and de-puffing. Research on sauna focuses on cardiovascular health rather than the face.

summary: Heat and steam sessions folded into skincare and wellness routines; the research is about the heart, not the face.
note: Alcohol, dehydration and certain heart conditions raise risk.
currentQuick:
Sauna and steam use is a heat-exposure habit that some people in looksmaxxing circles add for skin and general wellbeing.
Research is largely observational and about cardiovascular health. Little has tested facial appearance.
How it works: Heat raises skin temperature and sweating and acts as a mild heat stress on the body [1].
Risks and caveats: Dehydration, burns and cardiovascular strain are reported hazards, especially combined with alcohol or heart disease [1].
deepLead:
A sauna is a heated room or bathhouse used for sweating, and the word comes from Finnish. Steam rooms, such as the hammam, are a related practice that runs cooler and at close to full humidity . In looksmaxxing communities, sauna and steam sessions are discussed as a lifestyle habit for "sweating", skin and general wellbeing.
Published research on sauna use has focused mainly on cardiovascular and general health rather than facial appearance. Finnish observational studies associate regular sauna use with lower cardiovascular risk, and the evidence for skin conditions is described as insufficient . No studies found for appearance outcomes specifically.

name: Coffee / green tea ritual

angle.text: Users drink coffee or green tea as a morning routine meant to reduce facial puffiness. Both contain caffeine, and green tea adds polyphenols such as EGCG. No study has tested the effect on the face.

summary: Caffeine drinks used as a de-puffing routine; no study has tested the face effect.
note: Caffeine affects sleep; high-dose tea extracts linked to liver injury.
currentQuick:
People drink coffee or green tea as a daily ritual intended to reduce puffiness.
Caffeine has a short-lived diuretic effect in non-habitual users, but no published trial has tested these drinks for facial appearance.
How it works: Caffeine blocks adenosine receptors and may increase urine output briefly; tolerance develops with regular use [2].
Risks and caveats: Caffeine can disrupt sleep. Concentrated green tea extracts have been associated with liver toxicity [1][2].
deepLead:
The coffee or green tea ritual refers to drinking caffeinated beverages as part of a routine aimed at reducing facial puffiness or improving appearance. Both beverages contain caffeine, and green tea also contains polyphenols such as EGCG .
Caffeine can briefly increase urine output after large single doses in people not accustomed to it, but regular users develop tolerance . Wikipedia reports that green tea polyphenols have no proven biological effects in humans and that health claims were not supported by sufficient evidence in a 2011 EFSA review . No studies found on drinking either beverage to reduce facial puffiness.

name: Thyroid/hypothyroid evaluation

angle.text: People with persistent facial puffiness check thyroid function because hypothyroidism is a recognized medical cause of a puffy face. It is a clinical workup rather than a cosmetic method.

summary: Checking thyroid function as a medical explanation for a puffy face; clinical, not cosmetic.
note: Diagnosis and treatment belong to clinicians.
currentQuick:
Thyroid evaluation is a blood-test workup for hypothyroidism, which can include facial puffiness among its signs.
Many cases have few symptoms, and facial puffiness has other causes too.
How it works: Low thyroid hormone can cause fluid-like buildup in the skin (myxedema) and other changes; TSH is the first screening test [1].
Risks and caveats: Treatment is with prescribed levothyroxine, with dose monitored by TSH [1].
deepLead:
Thyroid evaluation means testing for hypothyroidism, a condition in which the thyroid does not make enough hormone. In appearance discussions it is raised as a possible medical cause of a persistently puffy face .
Wikipedia lists a puffy face, particularly around the eyes, dry coarse skin, hair loss and loss of the outer eyebrows among signs of the condition, and describes a TSH blood test as the usual first step, with levothyroxine as standard treatment . Evaluation is a clinical matter, and the wiki documents what clinical sources report.

name: Alcohol cutting (quit drinking)

angle.text: Users cut or quit alcohol to reduce facial puffiness and improve skin. The effect of drinking on the face is little studied directly.

summary: Quitting or cutting alcohol for less puff and better skin; the face effect itself is little studied.
note: Heavy drinkers should not stop abruptly without medical advice.
currentQuick:
Cutting alcohol is a common recommendation in appearance communities for reducing puffiness.
Sources describe benefits for hydration, sleep and weight, but direct facial studies are lacking.
How it works: Alcohol suppresses vasopressin, promotes fluid loss, disrupts sleep and adds calories [1].
Risks and caveats: Withdrawal can be dangerous in dependent drinkers.
deepLead:
Alcohol cutting means reducing or stopping alcohol, which looksmaxxing communities discuss as a way to reduce facial puffiness and improve skin.
Wikipedia states that alcohol suppresses vasopressin and acts as a diuretic, and that stopping drinking can benefit skin appearance, sleep and weight, though that section relies partly on secondary sources . Alcohol flush reaction in people with ALDH2 variants is a separate phenomenon .

name: Facial icing with green tea ice cubes

note: Avoid prolonged ice contact with skin.

A TikTok-popularised routine of applying frozen green tea to the face.

How it works: Cold constricts blood vessels and slows flow locally; green tea adds polyphenols whose human effects are unproven [1][2].
Risks and caveats: Ice burns and skin irritation are possible; circulation disorders are listed contraindications for cold therapy [1].

Facial icing with green tea ice cubes is a social media skincare practice in which frozen brewed green tea is rubbed on the face, with proponents citing reduced puffiness and calmer skin.
No studies found on this practice. Wikipedia describes general cold therapy as agreed to relieve symptoms like swelling with study results that conflict, and notes that green tea compounds have no proven biological effects in humans .

name: Pulsed dye laser for stretch marks

angle.text: Skin-focused communities use pulsed dye laser on fresh red or purple stretch marks to reduce redness before they fade to white. Trials are small and results are not firmly established.

summary: A vascular laser aimed at fresh red stretch marks; trials are small and results are not firmly established.
note: Reviews cited by Wikipedia find no stretch-mark treatment clearly effective; PDL-specific data in the sources are sparse.
currentQuick:
Pulsed dye laser is an in-office treatment used on new red or purple stretch marks, where the laser targets the blood vessels that give the marks their colour.
Sources reviewed describe only a small registered trial comparing it with carboxytherapy; broader reviews cited by Wikipedia report no clearly effective stretch-mark treatment.
How it works: The laser light is absorbed by hemoglobin in the small vessels of early marks, which proponents say reduces the redness.
Risks and caveats: The sources reviewed give no safety data for this use. Laser procedures generally are performed by clinicians, and results for older white marks are described as more limited.
deepLead:
Pulsed dye laser (PDL) treatment for stretch marks (striae distensae) is an in-office procedure in which a laser emitting light absorbed by blood vessels is applied to early, red or purple stretch marks (striae rubra). It is discussed in looksmaxxing and skin-focused communities as a way to reduce the redness of newly formed marks before they fade to white.
Stretch marks form when the dermis is torn or stretched during pregnancy, growth spurts, or weight and muscle gain, and begin as reddish or purple lesions that later become pale and atrophic . Wikipedia's article on stretch marks, citing a 2014 systematic review, states that no treatment has been clearly shown to be useful once marks have formed, and it does not specifically discuss pulsed dye laser .
Published trial registrations show that PDL continues to be studied, for example against carboxytherapy in red stretch marks in a small 20-person study registered in 2024, with no results listed in the registry entry .
